title: 26 — Polars Deep Dive
html:
26 — Polars Deep Dive

The engine, the memory model, the file formats, and the query optimiser — with numbers.

18 §3 introduces Polars: expressions, lazy evaluation, why it beats pandas. This file assumes that and goes down a level. Every code block here was executed and every number measured on Polars 1.35.2, Python 3.12, 8 logical cores, Windows before being written down. Your machine will differ; the ratios travel.

1. The mental model in four sentences

  1. Data lives in Apache Arrow columnar buffers, not Python objects — so a column of 5M floats is one contiguous 40 MB block, not 5M boxed floats.
  2. You write expressions, which are descriptions of work. The engine decides how and in what order to run them.
  3. Independent expressions run on every core without you asking.
  4. scan_* builds a plan; read_* runs immediately. The plan is where the optimiser earns its keep.

Everything below is a consequence of those four.

2. Memory — what a frame actually costs

import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "trade_id":  pl.arange(0, 5_000_000, eager=True),          # Int64  -> 8 bytes
    "portfolio": pl.Series(["PF-A", "PF-B", "PF-C", "PF-D"] * 1_250_000),
    "ccy":       pl.Series(["GBP", "USD", "EUR", "JPY"] * 1_250_000),
    "notional":  pl.arange(0, 5_000_000, eager=True).cast(pl.Float64),   # 8 bytes
    "qty":       pl.arange(0, 5_000_000, eager=True).cast(pl.Int32) % 1000,  # 4 bytes
})

print(f"{df.estimated_size('mb'):.1f} MB")     # 128.7 MB

Measured: 128.7 MB for 5,000,000 × 5. The three numeric columns alone account for 95.4 MB (5M × (8 + 8 + 4)), so the two string columns cost about 33 MB between them.

2.1 Estimating before you load

Type Bytes per value
Int8/UInt8/Boolean 1
Int32/Float32/Date 4
Int64/Float64/Datetime 8
String ~4 + the bytes, via a view + buffer
Categorical/Enum 4 per row + one copy of each distinct value
Any nullable column + 1 bit per row for the validity mask

Rule of thumb: sum the fixed widths, add string bytes, add ~10% for validity and padding. For anything else, estimated_size() is authoritative and free.

2.2 ⚠️ Categorical is not automatically smaller

cat = df.with_columns(pl.col("portfolio").cast(pl.Categorical),
                      pl.col("ccy").cast(pl.Categorical))
print(f"{cat.estimated_size('mb'):.1f} MB")    # 133.5 MB — LARGER than 128.7

Four distinct 4-character values do not benefit: Polars' string layout is already compact, and the categorical adds a 4-byte code per row plus dictionary bookkeeping. Categorical pays off when the strings are long and the cardinality is low relative to row count — country names across 50M rows, not currency codes across 5M.

Use Enum rather than Categorical when you know the set up front: it is cheaper (no global string cache) and it validates, so an unexpected value is an error rather than a silently new category.

2.3 Chunks and rechunk

Appending frames leaves a column split across several buffers. Most operations handle that, but some copy to make it contiguous first.

combined = pl.concat([a, b, c])      # chunked
combined = combined.rechunk()        # one contiguous buffer per column — costs a copy, pays back on repeated scans
print(combined.n_chunks())

Rechunk once after building, never inside a loop.

3. Cores — what parallelises, and what does not

import polars as pl, os
print(pl.thread_pool_size(), os.cpu_count())   # 8 8

Polars sizes its Rust thread pool to your core count at import. It is fixed once the module is imported — to change it, set the environment variable before the import:

import os
os.environ["POLARS_MAX_THREADS"] = "4"     # must precede `import polars`
import polars as pl

What runs in parallel

Work Parallel?
Each expression in select / with_columns / agg ✔ across threads
Reading multiple Parquet row groups or files ✔
group_by — partitioned hash aggregation ✔
Joins — build and probe phases ✔
sort ✔
map_elements (a Python lambda per row) ✘ GIL-bound, single-threaded
map_batches with a Python function ✘ per batch, though batches are handled natively

⚠️ The single biggest performance mistake in Polars is map_elements. It drops you back into the interpreter per row, holds the GIL, and disables every optimisation. If you find yourself reaching for it, the answer is almost always an expression — when/then/otherwise, a str/dt/list namespace method, or a join against a lookup frame.

Set POLARS_MAX_THREADS=1 when benchmarking a single-threaded baseline, or when running Polars inside a web request handler that is already parallel across requests — eight threads per request on an eight-core box is contention, not throughput.

4. Reading files

4.1 scan_* versus read_*

df   = pl.read_parquet("trades.parquet")    # loads now, returns DataFrame
lazy = pl.scan_parquet("trades.parquet")    # returns LazyFrame, reads nothing yet

Default to scan_*. It lets the optimiser push filters and column selection into the reader, so you read less from disk. read_* is right when the file is small, or when you genuinely need every row and column in memory.

4.2 CSV — the awkward one

df = pl.read_csv(
    "trades.csv",
    try_parse_dates=True,                       # ISO dates -> Date/Datetime instead of String
    schema_overrides={"amount": pl.Float32,      # beat inference where you know better
                      "account": pl.String},     # stop "007" becoming 7
    null_values=["", "NULL", "N/A"],
    ignore_errors=False,                         # keep this False; see below
    infer_schema_length=10_000,                  # None = scan the whole file
)

⚠️ Schema inference reads only the first infer_schema_length rows (1,000 by default). A column that is integer for 50,000 rows and then contains "N/A" will be inferred Int64 and blow up — or, with ignore_errors=True, silently become null. ignore_errors is how a data-quality problem becomes a silent wrong number. Prefer an explicit schema_overrides.

4.3 Every reader

Format Eager Lazy Notes
Parquet read_parquet scan_parquet The default choice. Pushdown, statistics, compression
CSV read_csv scan_csv Slowest; no types, no statistics
NDJSON read_ndjson scan_ndjson One JSON object per line — streamable
JSON read_json — Whole document; no lazy variant
Arrow IPC / Feather read_ipc scan_ipc Fastest round trip; no compression by default, so files are large
Delta Lake read_delta scan_delta Needs deltalake; gives time travel
Iceberg scan_iceberg ✔ Needs pyiceberg
Database read_database_uri — Via ConnectorX; fast, but materialises
Excel read_excel — Needs fastexcel/xlsx2csv

4.4 Globs and multiple files

lazy = pl.scan_parquet("data/trades/*.parquet")            # all matching files, read in parallel
lazy = pl.scan_parquet(["a.parquet", "b.parquet"])         # explicit list

⚠️ A glob requires every matched file to share a schema. Point one at a directory that also contains an aggregate output and you get:

SchemaError: extra column in file outside of expected schema: trade_id

That is a real error from writing this note — the glob picked up a sink output alongside the source files. Either keep outputs in a separate directory (do this) or pass extra_columns="ignore".

4.5 Hive partitioning

df.write_parquet("data/by_ccy", partition_by=["ccy"])
# -> data/by_ccy/ccy=GBP/…  ccy=USD/…  ccy=EUR/…  ccy=JPY/…

lazy = pl.scan_parquet("data/by_ccy", hive_partitioning=True)
lazy.filter(pl.col("ccy") == "GBP")     # skips three of four directories — never opens those files

The partition column comes back as a real column even though it exists only in the path. Partition on something with low cardinality that you filter on constantly — date, region, currency. Partitioning on trade_id produces millions of tiny files and is far slower than not partitioning at all.

5. Parquet, properly

5.1 The physical layout

trades.parquet
├── Row group 0        ← unit of parallelism AND of skipping
│   ├── Column chunk: trade_id   [Page][Page]…  + min/max/null statistics
│   ├── Column chunk: portfolio  [Dictionary page][Data page]…
│   └── …
├── Row group 1
└── Footer  ← schema + every row group's statistics, read first

The reader loads the footer, sees each row group's min/max per column, and can discard entire row groups before reading a byte of data.

5.2 What it looks like in practice

Writing the 5M-row frame:

df.write_parquet("trades.parquet", compression="zstd",
                 row_group_size=500_000, statistics=True)

Measured: 10.9 MB on disk versus 128.7 MB in memory — about 12× compression, in 10 row groups. Per column in row group 0:

Column Encoding Compressed size Statistics
trade_id PLAIN, RLE 533 kB 0 .. 499999
portfolio RLE_DICTIONARY ~0 kB PF-A .. PF-D
ccy RLE_DICTIONARY ~0 kB EUR .. USD
notional PLAIN, RLE 500 kB 0.0 .. 749998.5
qty RLE_DICTIONARY 4 kB 0 .. 999

Two 5M-row string columns cost essentially nothing on disk, because dictionary encoding stores four distinct values plus run lengths. This is the single strongest argument for Parquet over CSV on categorical-heavy data.

5.3 Compression

Codec Ratio Speed Use when
zstd best fast Default choice. Level 1–3 covers almost everything
snappy modest fastest Maximum read throughput, disk is cheap
lz4 modest fastest Similar to snappy; good interop
gzip good slow Only for consumers that demand it
uncompressed — — Scratch files on fast local disk

5.4 Row-group size is the tuning knob

Too small (< 100k rows) Too large (> 5M rows)
Footer bloat, many tiny reads Skipping is coarse — a filter hitting one row cannot skip its group
Poor compression per chunk Higher peak memory per reader thread

512k–1M rows is a good default. Match it to how you filter: if you always query one day, make a row group roughly one day.

5.5 Pushdown, measured

# Reads everything
pl.read_parquet(path)["notional"].sum()                                     # 122 ms

# Predicate pushdown — filter reaches the reader, most row groups skipped
(pl.scan_parquet(path)
   .filter(pl.col("trade_id") >= 4_500_000)
   .select(pl.col("notional").sum())
   .collect())                                                              #  32 ms

# Projection pushdown — one column of five leaves disk
pl.scan_parquet(path).select(pl.col("notional").sum()).collect()            #  36 ms

About 4× faster from pushdown alone, on a file that fits comfortably in memory. On a file that does not, the difference is between working and not.

⚠️ Pushdown only skips row groups when the data is clustered by the filtered column. trade_id is sorted here, so >= 4_500_000 matches one row group. Filter on a column whose values are scattered evenly and every row group's min/max spans the predicate — nothing is skipped, and only projection pushdown helps. Sort by your common filter key before writing. That single decision is worth more than any compression setting.

5.6 CSV versus Parquet, same data

CSV Parquet (zstd)
Size on disk 145.5 MB 10.9 MB
Full read 204 ms 91 ms
Column subset impossible — parse everything reads only what you asked for
Types inferred, fragile in the schema
Statistics none per row group

6. The lazy engine

6.1 Read the plan

plan = (pl.scan_parquet("trades.parquet")
          .filter(pl.col("ccy") == "GBP")
          .select(["portfolio", "notional"])
          .group_by("portfolio")
          .agg(pl.col("notional").sum()))

print(plan.explain())

AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false]
  [col("notional").sum()] BY [col("portfolio")]
  FROM
  simple π 2/2 ["portfolio", "notional"]
    Parquet SCAN [trades.parquet]
    PROJECT 3/5 COLUMNS
    SELECTION: [(col("ccy")) == ("GBP")]
    ESTIMATED ROWS: 5000000

Read it bottom-up. PROJECT 3/5 COLUMNS — only three of five columns are read, even though the final result uses two, because ccy is needed for the filter. SELECTION: inside the scan node is the filter having been pushed into the reader. That is the optimiser working; if your filter is not on the scan node, something blocked it.

6.2 What the optimiser does

Optimisation Effect
Predicate pushdown Filter at the file / row-group level
Projection pushdown Read only required columns
Slice pushdown head(n) stops the scan early
Common subexpression elimination Compute a repeated subexpression once
Simplify expressions Constant folding, dead branch removal
Join reordering Smaller side becomes the build side

Things that block pushdown: map_elements (opaque to the optimiser), a filter written after a group_by that depends on the aggregate, and anything forced through collect() mid-pipeline.

6.3 Where the time went

result, timings = plan.profile()      # timings: node, start, end (microseconds)

profile() is the first thing to reach for when a pipeline is slower than expected — it attributes time per node rather than leaving you guessing.

7. Streaming and sinks — larger than memory

# Whole result must fit in memory
out = plan.collect()

# Batched execution — bounded memory
out = plan.collect(engine="streaming")

# Never materialise at all: stream straight to a file
plan.sink_parquet("agg.parquet")
plan.sink_csv("agg.csv")

Measured on a 40M-row file — 68 MB on disk, 725 MB uncompressed — grouping to four rows:

Approach Peak working set Time
Baseline (interpreter + import) 38 MB —
read_parquet then group 1362 MB 557 ms
scan_parquet → collect() 1020 MB 385 ms
scan_parquet → collect(engine="streaming") 835 MB 355 ms

⚠️ Streaming cut peak memory by 39%, not by 10×. Be suspicious of claims otherwise. Polars still reads row groups in parallel across all eight threads, so several decompressed buffers are live at once. Streaming's real value is that peak stays bounded as the file grows — the eager number scales with file size, the streaming number scales with row-group size × thread count.

To genuinely cap memory on a huge input: fewer threads, smaller row groups, and sink_* rather than collect.

8. Data processing cookbook

Every snippet below was executed against a real frame.

8.1 Derive, classify, aggregate

result = (
    df
    .with_columns(
        band=pl.when(pl.col("notional") > 1_000_000).then(pl.lit("large"))
              .when(pl.col("notional") >   100_000).then(pl.lit("medium"))
              .otherwise(pl.lit("small")),
        month=pl.col("trade_date").dt.strftime("%Y-%m"),
    )
    .group_by("portfolio", "month")
    .agg(
        total      = pl.col("notional").sum(),
        trades     = pl.len(),
        biggest    = pl.col("notional").max(),
        large_only = pl.col("notional").filter(pl.col("band") == "large").mean(),
    )
    .sort("portfolio", "month")
)

Note pl.col(...).filter(...) inside agg — a conditional aggregate without a second pass or a subquery.

8.2 Window functions — aggregate without collapsing rows

df.with_columns(
    pct_of_portfolio = pl.col("notional") / pl.col("notional").sum().over("portfolio"),
    rank_in_ccy      = pl.col("notional").rank("dense", descending=True).over("ccy"),
    running_total    = pl.col("notional").cum_sum().over("portfolio"),
)

.over(...) is PARTITION BY. The frame keeps every row; the aggregate is broadcast back across the group.

8.3 Joins

left.join(right, on="k", how="inner")   # matched rows only
left.join(right, on="k", how="left")    # all left rows, nulls where unmatched
left.join(right, on="k", how="full")    # everything from both sides
left.join(right, on="k", how="semi")    # left rows THAT HAVE a match — no columns added
left.join(right, on="k", how="anti")    # left rows with NO match — the "what's missing" query
left.join(right, how="cross")           # cartesian product

semi and anti are the ones people forget and then reimplement badly with a join plus a null check. anti is the cleanest possible reconciliation-break query.

# As-of join: for each fill, the most recent quote at or before it
fills.sort("t").join_asof(quotes.sort("t"), on="t", strategy="backward")

⚠️ join_asof requires both sides sorted on the join key. It silently gives wrong answers otherwise — sort explicitly rather than assuming.

8.4 Time series

ts.group_by_dynamic("ts", every="1d").agg(pl.col("v").sum())      # resample to daily buckets
ts.with_columns(pl.col("v").rolling_mean(window_size=3))          # trailing 3-period mean
ts.upsample("ts", every="12h").fill_null(strategy="forward")      # fill gaps in a series

8.5 Reshaping

df.pivot(on="ccy", index="portfolio", values="notional", aggregate_function="sum")
df.unpivot(index="trade_id", on=["notional", "qty"])               # wide -> long
df.explode("tags")                                                 # one row per list element
df.select(pl.struct(["a", "b"]).alias("nested"))                    # pack columns into a struct

8.6 Nulls and types

df.null_count()                                   # per-column null counts — first thing on new data
df.fill_null(0)                                   # or strategy="forward" / "mean"
df.drop_nulls(subset=["notional"])
pl.Series(["1", "x", "3"]).cast(pl.Int64, strict=False)   # -> [1, null, 3] rather than raising
df.describe()                                     # count/null_count/mean/std/min/max/quartiles
df.glimpse()                                      # wide frames, readable

9. Interop

arrow = df.to_arrow()          # zero copy — same Arrow buffers, no serialisation
back  = pl.from_arrow(arrow)   # zero copy
pdf   = df.to_pandas()         # COPIES unless use_pyarrow_extension_array=True
npy   = df["notional"].to_numpy()   # zero copy for a numeric column with no nulls

Arrow is the lingua franca — DuckDB, pandas 2.x, PyArrow and Polars can hand each other the same buffers without serialising. Crossing to pandas' classic block manager, or to NumPy from a nullable column, forces a copy.

10. Traps

Trap Why it hurts Do this
map_elements Single-threaded, per-row interpreter, blocks the optimiser Use expressions
collect() mid-pipeline Materialises and discards the plan Collect once, at the end
read_* when scan_* would do No pushdown; reads everything scan_* by default
ignore_errors=True on CSV Turns a data problem into silent nulls schema_overrides
Filtering on an unclustered column No row groups skipped Sort by the filter key before writing
Categorical everywhere Can increase memory Measure; prefer Enum for known sets
Globbing a mixed-schema directory SchemaError Keep outputs elsewhere
join_asof on unsorted input Wrong answers, no error Sort both sides explicitly
Eight threads inside a web request Contention across concurrent requests POLARS_MAX_THREADS before import

11. Checklist

Before shipping a Polars pipeline:

  • scan_* rather than read_*, with a single collect/sink at the end
  • explain() shows the filter on the scan node and PROJECT n/m COLUMNS with n < m
  • Written as Parquet with zstd, ~512k-row row groups, sorted by the common filter key
  • Partitioned only on low-cardinality columns you actually filter on
  • No map_elements anywhere in the hot path
  • CSV inputs have an explicit schema_overrides; ignore_errors is False
  • Peak memory measured on production-shaped data, not on a sample
  • sink_* used when the output does not need to be in memory

Interview angle. "Why is Polars faster than pandas?" has a bad answer and a good one. The bad one is "it's written in Rust". The good one: "Columnar Arrow memory so operations are cache-friendly and vectorised; multi-threaded by default; and a lazy optimiser that pushes filters and column selection into the file reader, so on Parquet it often reads a fraction of the data. Rust is why there is no GIL in the way — it isn't the reason on its own."
